You should trade sidebar links with @newfatmike .

Sent him a PM yesterday and there was a link to it in the sidebar of /v/vaping this morning - good deal, thanks for the recommendation. Hopefully we can get a bit more traffic here, I'd love to see the local DIY community grow.

The CA kills coils and some people complain about it killing their throats. You have a few options here...

You can lower the amount of CA and it will still taste good, or you can lower the dragon fruit to 2% and add 1% quince. The quince will give you the tartness without killing your throat, and will show a bit more mercy on your coils. But the key to this is letting it steep for a week or so.

The other thing in this recipe that kills coils is that damn yellow food coloring in the Banana Cream. You have to use the LA stuff or else it won't taste quite right. But...if you can get your hands on some colorless LA banana cream, your coils will thank you. TBD Liquids sells colorless - 4oz for $12.99.

On a side note, if you're gonna order that colorless BC from TBD, order some of his juice too. It's pretty damn good. :)

EDIT: One more thing...if you go overboard on the quince, or think it's harsh, you can add a couple of drops (per 30ml) of TFA smooth. It will round it out a bit.

In some ways he reminds me of David Mamet, in the way he can use the character's speech to transcend the traditional need for exposition or scene setting. I can't read works by either of those guys without being depressed by my own writing. I wish my characters came alive like that.

Brandon Sanderson is an incredible writer. I started buying his books in a very haphazard way and haven't been disappointed once.

Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy. A combination of humour, and science fiction that influenced my sense of humour more then any other book series. Was quoting it for years, had a family member's copy of the "trilogy of four", with four different images, including an old Douglas Adams self-portrait using an old Mac. It also led me to be shell shocked when I found out about Mostly Harmless, especially as So Long ends on such a great note. Cast of characters that can only really be experienced first hand to describe. *EDIT: Deleted some words, my love of H2G2 is such that it makes me forget to proofread.

I came here to say Hitchhiker's Guide, and I'm glad to see that it's already here. These books are hilarious and entertaining, and Douglas Adams had the incredible ability to create characters that you could love, hate, laugh at, cry with, etc. The dialogue he wrote is wonderful and witty, and there is always plenty of it. Just talking about this series is giving me the urge to read it yet another time.

Yeah, this thread particularly has been pushing me to rethink about when to do another reread. it is the constant "it has been much too long since I read the series" versus "I have X free time during the week, Y books that I have been meaning to read".

"Yeah. Listen, I'm Zaphod Beeblebrox, my father was Zaphod Beeblebrox the Second and my grandfather was Zaphod Beeblebrox the Third.... There was an accident with a contraceptive and a time machine."

It has to be Feits' Riftwar Saga;

Hyperion cantos. it's fascinating stuff. Something about current world religion mixing with far off times scifi that draws me in.

Simmon's other books Illium and Olympus are also notable for their mix of history and sci fi that just gets me going.
I'm loving the new Queen of the Tearling so much and I don't know why.

Hannibal Letter series by Thomas Harris, although not so much "Hannibal Rising." Harris wrote that one under duress, and it shows.

His Dark Materials by Phillip Pullman.

this book broke my heart. it was an amazing ride.

The Dark Tower series by Stephen King.

I loved 4, but 5 and six were my least favorite. For me, it's the overall story tho, I can forgive some of the more "boring" or slow parts of the series. I love The Belgariad by David Eddings. It's good for any age, it has something for everyone, and I can read it over and over and it never gets old. It's perfectly paced and well written, and I've never found a series like it.

Robin Hobb's Farseer, Tawny Man, and Soldier Son trilogies.

The Gormenghast trilogy by Melvyn Peake.

Roger Zelany, Amber Series features unique and descriptive worlds. Reminds me a little bit like a created string theory adventure.
The Discworld series by Sir Terry Pratchett. Brandon Sanderson explains 'why' better than I could.

The Amber series by Roger Zelazny. I read it as a young teenager and it got me hooked on sci-fi. It also got me hooked on being an avid reader, and I haven't looked back. It's very entertaining, funny, moving, and what's you wonder how someone came up with something like that.

David Gemmell's books. Heroic fantasy at its best. I know you asked for a series and although they aren't technically, there are characters that cross over and pass though in other books, sometimes getting prequels later on (if that makes sense).

James Barclay's 'Chronicals of the raven' and 'Legends of thr raven'. Again heroic fantasy but for me, these books make me feel as though I was being taken on a journey. The event that were happening we're always interesting and well paced often unexpected. (And not that it should matter but, when I bought these soft back versions They look great, solid colour cover with black, and the edge of the pages were in the same colour. Very happy to have them on my shelf)

And finally, Katherin Kerr's Daggerspell. It's been years since I read them. Again these are fantasy, and though out the series there are many charecters in different forms woven together though events in the past that only one of them knows of, he has to set things right but if often faced with situations that cant be. parts of these books were quite emotional and moved me to tears at one point (yup, iw as younger but i still say that is a sign of awesome writing/storytelling!)

If any of you pick them up I hope you enjoy them as much as I did

Either Timothy Zahn's Thrawn Trilogy, or the Jeeves and Wooster books by PG Wodehouse.

The Thrawn Trilogy because I'm a big fan of Star Wars, and I feel those novels perfectly captured the tone and, more importantly, the pacing of the original films. They were the starting point of the Star Wars Expanded Universe. It's a shame the timeline they exist in is no longer canon, but I'm hopeful as to what the new films can bring to the table. Them not being consided Canon doesn't diminish my love of them one bit.

The Jeeves and Wooster books are simply fun to read. They're short, irreverant and entertaining. The double act of Jeeves and Wooster (expertly depicted by Fry and Laurie on television) play so well together, and the stories are always enjoyable. There's never a dull moment, and they always cheer me up. My personal favourite is Aunts Aren't Gentlemen.
Hemingway is one of my favorite authors. He's has an incredible economy of words and while it takes a bit to get used to it's amazing how much depth he packs into each short story.

The Commonwealth Saga and The Void Trilogy by Peter F. Hamilton.

This universe is possibly my favourite sci-fi universe. So many complex and intricate storylines that fall into place like pieces of a puzzle when the author wants it to. In the Void Trilogy there is another universe inside the universe, and it's pretty much middle ages with telekinesis, which turns out to be pretty awesome too.
Tales of Earthsea. Ursula le Guin. Really engrossing, something to escape reality with.

The Manifold Trilogy by Stephen Baxter. No other sci-fi I've read even remotely compares, although the third book Origin is the weakest. If Voat had a tagging feature you may as well tag me as 'the Baxter guy.' I'm sorta close to finishing is entire works.
No Redwall? Shame on all of you.

The Dune series by Frank Herbert.

Just talking about the original six books. Dune was such a great story I tend to re-read it every few years or so. Sometimes I'll pick up one of the others and re-read them too. I think the 2nd book (Dune Messiah) was the weakest of the series with some cringe-worthy moments. I know a lot of people dislike the 4th (God Emperor Of Dune), but that one has grown on me over the years. The last two books were great too!

Just because it has such a special place in my heart: The Dragonlance Chronicles by Margaret Weis and Tracy Hickman. I was book-phobic as a kid and hated reading, they just scared me. I loved video games, especially fantasy RPGs, so my dad (who loves reading) sat me down and handed me the first in the series knowing I'd love it if I actually sat and read it. He specifically grabbed the edition where it was split into 6 smaller books instead of the larger trilogy so I wouldn't be intimidated.

I ended up finishing it in a couple days and made him go buy me the rest. I still have multiple copies of each book and read them when I'm feeling stressed or burnt out.

Wheel of Time.

Loved it for the same reason I delayed reading it for so long. It's dense. There is just so much of it. It was intimidating at first, but once I started it I couldn't put it down.

The Millennium saga by Stieg Larsson. Those three books left such an indelible mark on me. I loved the characters, especially Lisbeth Salander who is my favorite female heroine in fiction. Each book had such a dark, gritty feel to them that made the book so compelling to me. I wished Larsson were still alive to continue the series.

I adore the trilogy, but it got a bit too over the top.

The English translation was fantastic though and the first book was amazing, second book still amazing, third book went a bit too far with political conspiracy, but was still a fun read.

I also wish he were still alive to see what direction he'd take the characters, especially after hearing he had an outline for something like eight or nine books.

I picked up Walter Moers' first book in the loosely-affiliated-but-not-actually-sequential-series of Zammonia books because I liked the cover described it as a mix of J.K. Rowling, Shel Silverstein and Douglas Adams. It was exactly that. I read the other three over the next year. Highly recommended, Moers' imagination is pretty bonkers.

what's a normal work day like as an IT security auditor?

I either write documents or go to clients. The clients are mostly big or medium companies. I investigate clients' IT infrastructure, systems and business processes, talk with business managers and system administrators. Then I go to my office and write reports on what I've investigated, analyze the system, infrastructure.

When there's no work I learn sth new on IT security. Or just browse the web.

For many people looks like Russia is the crib of amazing programmers and security experts. Why do you have this profound interest about technology? Other countries have his experts too, but the impression I have is that russians embrace this style of life like no other.

Here we have (well, had, the goverment just destroys it) strong educational system from school to PhD. That's why our specialists are good. And going to uni is like one of necessary steps for an average man, if you haven't finished a university in your mid 20s there must be sth wrong with you. That's what differs Russia from other countries.

Also half of a year (in some regions up to 11 months) are not suitable for going out, leisuring on a beach, you know.. so we have to sit at home and have fun with computers.

And, moreover, there is a, like, strong security tradition here (don't know how to say better) from the soviet times. The secrets are overwhelmingly guarded. So there is an actual need for those experts. Nowadays the government makes new and new laws of diffferent necesserity and quality that make a headache for business and citizens and new work for security experts, increasing the need of security experts. I think no country guards its secrets better than Russia.
